Experiments that changed questions

One dollar or twenty: cognitive dissonance

Those paid less to lie ended up believing the lie more. A classic 1959 experiment.

In 1959, Leon Festinger and James Carlsmith asked students to spend an hour on very boring tasks, such as turning pegs a quarter turn over and over. Afterwards they were paid to tell the next participant that the task had been interesting.

The less pay, the more conviction

Some were paid one dollar and others twenty. In the end, those paid one dollar rated the task as more enjoyable than those paid twenty. Why? Those paid twenty had a good reason to lie. Those paid one did not, and to reduce the discomfort of having said something they did not believe, they changed what they believed.

Festinger called that discomfort cognitive dissonance. It helps explain why we justify costly decisions, why we value more what took effort, and why it is so hard to admit a mistake.

References

  1. Festinger, L. y Carlsmith, J. M. (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58(2), 203–210.
